description: Technologists are over-interviewed about the new and under-interviewed about the durable. Ask about maintenance, legacy systems, incidents, and judgment, and you will get material nobody else is getting.

questions.text: What is the oldest system you depend on, and what happens when it finally goes?
questions.lands_because: Legacy dependency is the actual condition of the industry and almost never the subject of an interview. It produces both a great story and a real insight.

questions.text: Walk me through an incident. Not the postmortem version - what the first twenty minutes actually felt like.
questions.lands_because: Rejecting the sanitized postmortem is what unlocks it. Incident response is genuinely dramatic and technologists rarely get asked for the experience rather than the writeup.
followups: Who was in the channel, and who should have been?
What did the postmortem leave out?

questions.text: What technical decision are you living with that you would make differently now?
questions.lands_because: Technical debt as autobiography. Engineers are unusually honest about this because owning a bad call is high-status among peers.
followups: Was it wrong then, or only wrong later?

questions.text: What does your team spend time on that produces no visible output but would be catastrophic to stop?
questions.lands_because: Names the maintenance and reliability work that never appears in a roadmap or a launch post, which is most of what keeps software alive.
followups: How do you justify that work upward?

questions.text: Where in your work does the current wave of AI tooling actually help, and where does it quietly create work?
questions.lands_because: The two-sided framing gets past both boosterism and dismissal to a practitioner's real ledger, which is what listeners actually want.
followups: What has it changed about how you hire or train juniors?

questions.text: Who in your organization can veto an engineering decision, and should they be able to?
questions.lands_because: Gets at the real authority structure between engineering, product, security, and legal - the source of most of the frustration and most of the interesting stories.
followups: Tell me about a time that veto was right.
